variants.name: View trait object (&mut dyn View)
variants.idiom_name: trait View + presenter struct holding &mut dyn View (object-safe, dynamic dispatch)
variants.implementation_notes: Rust has no classes, so the view contract is a trait and the presenter a struct: the dynamic-dispatch form takes &mut dyn View, which keeps the presenter's type non-generic, allows switching view implementations at runtime, and costs one vtable indirection per call. The model stays a separate struct and the presenter is the only code holding both. There is no direct replacement for the classic structure - traits map onto interfaces - but the borrow checker changes the architecture: the presenter cannot hold a long-lived mutable reference to a widget tree that also mutates itself, so views are usually driven from outside the presenter's borrow scope. Prefer this form when several view types must be substituted at runtime or code size matters.
pitfalls: The borrow checker rejects the OO habit of two-way references: the caller cannot hold &mut view while the presenter does; scope one mutable borrow at a time or move the view into the presenter.

Trait objects require object safety: generic methods or Self-returning signatures must be reshaped, and the trait needs a lifetime/ownership decision (Box<dyn View>, &mut dyn View, Rc<RefCell<dyn View>>).
Rc<RefCell<dyn View>> makes the code compile but moves borrow errors to runtime panics; prefer exclusive &mut references and explicit ownership.

variants.name: Monomorphized generic presenter (V: View)
variants.idiom_name: struct Presenter<V: View> or fn run<V: View> with static dispatch and no vtable
variants.implementation_notes: The static-dispatch form makes the presenter generic over the view type (Presenter<V: View>), so each concrete screen monomorphizes its own code with no vtable and no dynamic lifetime; this is the shape the Rust book recommends when the set of implementations is fixed at compile time. It trades flexibility - one presenter type per view type and larger binaries - for speed and simpler ownership, because the concrete view can be owned by value. Choose it for embedded or performance-sensitive HMIs with a fixed widget set; choose the dyn form when views are swapped at runtime or the presenter must be stored in a collection.
pitfalls: Every generic instantiation compiles its own copy: a large presenter used with many view types grows the binary and compile time; keep the generic boundary thin or box the view.
Trait bounds spread through call sites; if the view type escapes into public APIs, the bound must be repeated or the type boxed, which is where the dyn form becomes simpler.
The concrete view is owned by value here, so it cannot also be borrowed by the toolkit's event loop; coordinate ownership with the GUI framework's model (handle-based or closure-driven).
